CS540 MATMUL WALKTHROUGH — ILLUSTRATIVE PLACEHOLDERS

No compilation or assembly capture was performed. Only the Python excerpt is
actual course source; every lowered representation is an authored teaching sketch.
Source excerpt adapted from Tenstorrent TT-Lang; Apache-2.0 (see bundled license).

Kernel: matmul.py; A[64,128], B[128,96], out[64,96]; BF16; grid(1,1).
One-tile blocks, queue depth2; selected output C_tile[1,2].

0 · Source and specialization
matmul.py · exact compute-kernel excerpt

@ttl.compute()
def compute():
    for _ in range(Mt):
        for _ in range(Nt):
            with out_dfb.reserve() as out_blk:
                acc = ttl.block.fill(0, shape=out_blk.shape)
                for _ in range(Kt):
                    with a_dfb.wait() as a_blk, b_dfb.wait() as b_blk:
                        acc += a_blk @ b_blk
                out_blk.store(acc)

The source is matmul(a,b,out), with A[64,128], B[128,96], and C[64,96]. Each queue has
two slots, and each slot holds one 32×32 BF16 tile. The tile counts are therefore Mt=2,
Nt=3, and Kt=4.

Follow output C_tile[1,2]. Its accumulator starts at zero and receives four tile
products. Across all six outputs, each input queue supplies 24 blocks and the output
queue supplies six. The frontend specializes the source using tensor metadata and
captured configuration; tensor values remain runtime inputs.

1 · Python control flow and TTL IR
PLACEHOLDER · initial TTL sketch · abbreviated MLIR notation

// PLACEHOLDER: illustrative structure, NOT a compiler dump.
// Each input block type is tensor<1x1x!ttcore.tile<32x32,bf16>>.
// Types/attributes/constant definitions omitted; ACC_T is unresolved.
scf.for %m = %c0 to %c2 step %c1 {
  scf.for %n = %c0 to %c3 step %c1 {
    %out = ttl.cb_reserve ...
    %zero = <zero block from ttl.block.fill>
    %final = scf.for %k = %c0 to %c4 step %c1
        iter_args(%acc = %zero) -> (<ACC_T>) {
      %a = ttl.cb_wait ...
      %b = ttl.cb_wait ...
      %product = ttl.matmul %a, %b ...
      %next = ttl.add %acc, %product ...
      ttl.cb_pop ...  // release A after its use
      ttl.cb_pop ...  // release B after its use
      scf.yield %next : <ACC_T>
    }
    ttl.store %final, %out ...
    ttl.cb_push ...
  }
}

In Python, acc += ... reassigns a variable. In SSA form, the K loop receives an
accumulator value, computes its successor, and yields that value to the next iteration.
After the fourth iteration, the loop result is stored in the output block. Replacing
this recurrence with four independent stores would lose the earlier products.

The with scopes become buffer operations as well. Acquiring an input waits for a
published block, and leaving its scope releases it. The output reservation spans the
whole K loop, so publication occurs after the reduction. SSA names identify values;
allocation passes later decide where to store them.

2 · Block arithmetic to tile computation
PLACEHOLDER · compute/tile representation · explanatory notation

// PLACEHOLDER: local recipe for ONE acquired A/B block pair.
// The outer source K loop still has four iterations.
local tile iteration extent = (m_local=1, n_local=1, k_local=1)
A map: (m_local,n_local,k_local) -> (m_local,k_local)
B map: (m_local,n_local,k_local) -> (k_local,n_local)
C map: (m_local,n_local,k_local) -> (m_local,n_local)
iterators = [parallel, parallel, reduction]

ttl.compute ... {
  %product = ttl.tile_matmul_block ...
  <accumulator update / tile store or yield, as selected by lowering>
}

One @ in this source multiplies a single A tile by a single B tile. Its local recipe has
one tile along each axis. The scalar dot products inside that tile have length 32; four
iterations of the outer K loop cover scalar K=128.

The compiler forms compute regions and introduces tile indexing maps and iterator kinds.
It also materializes intermediate values in buffers where their uses require storage.
Throughout this process, the outer loops still describe six outputs, each with four K
terms.

The separate 2×4 @ 4×3 block fixture in chapter 04 represents a larger block expression.
It covers the same matrix dimensions with a different block size and comes from an
independent compiler test.

3 · Accumulator and queue storage
PLACEHOLDER · resource plan · physical assignments await capture

PLACEHOLDER RESOURCE PLAN — NOT AN ALLOCATION DUMP
A queue:   1 tile/block × 2 blocks × 2,048 B = 4,096 B
B queue:   1 tile/block × 2 blocks × 2,048 B = 4,096 B
Out queue: 1 tile/block × 2 blocks × 2,048 B = 4,096 B
Declared queue payload:                         12,288 B

Accumulator across K:
  initial value: zero tile
  update: previous accumulator + A_tile @ B_tile
  storage strategy: <record actual DST or L1 decision>
  precision/configuration: <record actual compiler decision>

Physical CB indices/addresses: <capture later>
Compiler-created buffers:     <capture later>
DST slots and sync boundaries: <capture later>

The accumulator must survive all four K iterations. Recurrence analysis starts before
tile conversion; this stage groups its storage consequences for discussion. A DST
strategy and an L1 pack/reload strategy can differ in both traffic and numerical
behavior. A real capture is needed to identify the choice for this kernel.

The three declared BF16 queues occupy 12 KiB per core. That total excludes compiler-
created buffers, alignment, code, and runtime storage. Their logical names also do not
determine physical CB indices or addresses.

One output tile fits within the usual four-tile FP32 double-buffered DST section. The
allocator must still account for other live values and the selected configuration.
Inputs remain live through their last use, and the writer must finish its output
transfer before the output slot can be reused.

4 · TTKernel operations and synchronization
PLACEHOLDER · TTKernel operation families · partial ordering sketch

// PLACEHOLDER: representative operation families for this source.
reader:
  ttkernel.cb_reserve_back ...        // obtain input capacity
  <NoC reads for the selected A and B tiles>
  <read completion before publication>
  ttkernel.cb_push_back ...

compute:
  ttkernel.cb_wait_front ...          // acquire each input
  <DST acquire / accumulator restoration at selected boundaries>
  ttkernel.matmul_block ...           // one local tile product
  <lower the accumulator update and preserve its state>
  <commit / wait / pack / release at selected boundaries>
  ttkernel.cb_pop_front ...           // release consumed input

writer:
  ttkernel.cb_wait_front ...          // completed output only
  <NoC write and write completion>
  ttkernel.cb_pop_front ...

// Positions/counts of tile_regs_* and pack calls require actual IR.
// Output publication remains once per completed K reduction.

At this stage, buffer operations use circular-buffer APIs and arithmetic uses compute
APIs such as matmul_block. Source copy waits become transfer-completion operations;
scope exits become queue publication or release; output stores require materialization
and packing.

DST synchronization coordinates math and pack. Acquisition grants ownership, commit/wait
establishes the handoff, and release permits reuse. The selected accumulation strategy
determines where these operations appear, so the sketch leaves those boundaries
unresolved. Input and output block counts alone cannot tell us how many internal pack or
register-synchronization calls will be emitted.

Check the transfer boundaries too: the reader completes both input copies before
publishing, and the writer completes its copy before releasing the output slot.

5 · EmitC and device C++
PLACEHOLDER · C++ pseudocode · authored teaching outline

// PLACEHOLDER: source-level loop structure and API families only.
// Definitions, arguments, config, and exact accumulator path omitted.
void compute_kernel() {
  for (unsigned m = 0; m < 2; ++m) {
    for (unsigned n = 0; n < 3; ++n) {
      cb_reserve_back(/* output CB, one tile */);
      /* initialize accumulator using the selected storage strategy */
      for (unsigned k = 0; k < 4; ++k) {
        cb_wait_front(/* A CB, one tile */);
        cb_wait_front(/* B CB, one tile */);
        /* selected initialization, DST synchronization and restore */
        matmul_block(/* actual generated operands and tile arguments */);
        /* selected accumulation / materialization */
        cb_pop_front(/* A CB, one tile */);
        cb_pop_front(/* B CB, one tile */);
      }
      /* pack final result and finish its destination handoff */
      cb_push_back(/* output CB, one tile */);
    }
  }
}

EmitC represents calls, types, expressions, and control flow that can be translated to
C++. The resulting source is compiled with the target libraries and configuration. The
outline shows the original m, n, and k loops and representative API families; their
exact arguments and accumulator implementation await a real capture.

Reader and writer produce separate generated source, while compute code supports the
unpack, math, and pack control roles. Keep these identities when collecting the
corresponding binaries.

The device compiler may inline calls, fold constants, or unroll loops. Follow the output
values and their dependencies across these changes: the implementation must still
produce six output tiles from four K terms each.

6 · Device instructions
PLACEHOLDER · symbolic assembly outline · no ELF or disassembly captured

# PLACEHOLDER: NOT real disassembly; no addresses or encodings.
# One possible unrolled-or-looped K region, shown as a loop here.
# <...> marks unresolved code and register placeholders.

    <initialize k register to 0 and bound register to 4>
.L_k:
    <input wait / readiness implementation>
    <accumulator restore and DST synchronization, if required>
    <Tensix matrix-engine instruction-issue sequence>
    <accumulator update / preservation>
    <input-release implementation>
    addi <k_reg>, <k_reg>, 1
    blt  <k_reg>, <bound_reg>, .L_k
    <final packing and output publication>

# addi/blt illustrate scalar RISC-V loop control only.
# Actual code may use different branches or unroll the loop.
# Matrix instructions and exact synchronization await target capture.

The displayed addi and blt illustrate scalar RISC-V loop control. The matrix product is
issued to the Tensix compute machinery in the unresolved region. Its actual
instructions, registers, addresses, and synchronization sequence depend on the target
binary.

With a matching ELF, select a short region and map it back to generated C++ and the
accumulator path. Identify the processor role and distinguish instruction issue from the
wait or dependency that establishes completion. The compiler may also unroll the K loop,
so the loop shown here is only one possible structure.

No ELF was captured for this walkthrough. Instruction counts and timing must come from a
later compilation and execution, with the source, shape, flags, toolchain, and target
recorded together.
